citation: Dalgarno, Barney, & Mark J. W. Lee. (2010). What are the learning affordances of 3-D virtual environments? British Journal of Educational Technology, 41(1), 10–32. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2009.01038.x [version of record 2010; online-first © 2009; cited as 2010 by Fowler and CAMIL]
thesis: Isolating what is genuinely 3-D-specific about 3-D virtual learning environments, the paper synthesizes two decades of applied literature into ten distinguishing characteristics (representational fidelity; learner interaction) and derives five learning affordances (spatial knowledge representation, experiential tasks, motivation/engagement, contextualization/transfer, richer collaboration), integrating both into a model (Fig. 2) with identity/presence/co-presence as intermediate outcomes; explicitly rejects simple 2-D-vs-3-D media-comparison designs (after Clark) and proposes a research agenda testing the model's assumed links rather than asserting them as established.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: States the hype/evidence gap for 3-D VLEs versus 2-D equivalents and the paper's aim of isolating 3-D-specific distinguishing characteristics and deriving affordances (pp.10-11).

sections.title: 3-D VLEs
sections.summary: Defines 3-D VE via Wann & Mon-Williams (1996); distinguishes desktop from immersive VEs; synthesizes prior characteristic-frameworks into a two-category, ten-item taxonomy (representational fidelity; learner interaction); adopts Slater's immersion/presence distinction; treats presence, co-presence, identity as consequences not independent properties; presents Figure 1 initial model (pp.11-17).

sections.title: The learning affordances of 3-D VEs
sections.summary: Reviews applications across three categories (3-D simulations/microworlds; 3-D-as-interface; 3-D multi-user VLEs), deriving five numbered affordances: spatial knowledge, experiential tasks, motivation/engagement, contextualization/transfer, collaboration (pp.17-23).

sections.title: A model of learning in 3-D VLEs
sections.summary: Integrates characteristics and affordances into an elaborated model (Figure 2), with identity, presence, and co-presence as intermediate outcomes (p.23).

sections.title: Towards a research agenda: conclusion and recommendations
sections.summary: Characterizes existing evidence as anecdotal 'show-and-tell'; explicitly rejects simple 2-D-vs-3-D media-comparison designs on Clark's media-vs-method grounds; proposes a roadmap of research questions (Table 2) toward validating assumptions and deriving design principles (pp.23-25).

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: six sub-characteristics: realistic display, smooth view/object motion, consistent object behavior, user representation (avatar), spatial audio, kinaesthetic/tactile feedback; folds in Brna's 'social fidelity' for multi-user contexts

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: learner-interaction category: embodied actions (view control/navigation/manipulation), embodied verbal/non-verbal communication, control of environment attributes, construction/scripting of objects

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: adopts Slater's immersion (objective/system) vs presence (subjective) distinction; treats presence as a consequence of fidelity + interactivity, not an independent 3-D-VLE property

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: co-presence glossed as 'being there together'; explicit extension of the Short/Williams/Christie (1976) CMC social-presence tradition; treated as a consequence, not an independent property

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: avatar-mediated identity construction via Dickey's (2002) three aspects: presence, representation, embodiment

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: Affordance 3: personalization/choice-driven intrinsic motivation (Cordova & Lepper); game/narrative approaches

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: Affordance 3: invokes Csikszentmihalyi's (1990) flow construct directly, hypothesizing fidelity + natural interface increase likelihood of flow

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: Affordance 4: contextualization/transfer grounded in situated-learning theory (Lave & Wenger; Brown, Collins & Duguid)

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: Affordance 2: experiential tasks impractical/impossible in reality; nuclear-plant, astronaut, forestry-operator training examples

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: defined per Slater as objective/measurable system properties leading to presence; explicitly not treated as a unique property of 3-D VLEs

conditions.label: review / meta-analytic aggregate
conditions.design: conceptual/model synthesis across ~three decades of applied 3-D VE/VLE literature (no primary data collected); dozens of implemented systems cited as illustrative cases, not data-bearing studies

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.design: explicit primary object of the article ('desktop virtual environments... explored using standard PC hardware'); immersive VEs (HMD/CAVE) noted as historically cost-prohibitive and discussed only by extension

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.design: mentioned only as the immersive alternative to desktop VEs; not analyzed empirically or contrasted with desktop-3D in this source

conditions.label: methodological stance (not a media-condition column)
conditions.design: explicitly rejects controlled 2-D-vs-3-D media-comparison designs after Clark (1983, 1994a, 1994b) as unable to separate learning design from media; calls instead for research testing whether affordances are harnessed by design

readings.claim: 3-D VLEs are distinguished from other VLEs by three-dimensionality, smooth temporal change, and interactivity, elaborated into ten characteristics across representational fidelity and learner interaction.
Presence, co-presence, and identity construction are consequences of representational fidelity and learner interaction, not independent defining properties of 3-D VLEs.
Five learning affordances follow from the applications literature: spatial knowledge representation; experiential tasks; motivation/engagement; contextualization/transfer; richer collaboration.
The relationships between characteristics, intermediate outcomes, and affordances are assumptions requiring empirical validation; existing literature is largely anecdotal show-and-tell.

Media-comparison research designs (2-D vs 3-D holding learning design constant) are methodologically unsound per Clark's media-vs-method argument; research should instead test whether affordances are harnessed by learning design.
A research agenda linking 3-D VLE characteristics to design principles/best practice is contingent on first validating the model's assumed links.

tensions.axis: affordance-model theoretical optimism vs. media-comparison empirical skepticism
tensions.note: The paper itself supplies both poles: it derives five optimistic affordances from the applications literature while simultaneously arguing the evidentiary base for them is anecdotal and that the natural test (2-D vs 3-D comparison) is methodologically invalid — a tension this cluster's Strand C inherits and partially resolves via value-added (not media-comparison) designs.

tensions.axis: presence/co-presence as independent constructs (prior frameworks, e.g. Brna 1999) vs. presence/co-presence as consequences (this paper's own simplification)
tensions.note: Dalgarno & Lee deliberately depart from six-dimensional prior frameworks by demoting presence, co-presence, and identity to intermediate/consequent status rather than independent characteristics.
